core_themes.name: Fee variability and opacity
core_themes.claim: Letting agent fees to tenants vary considerably in amount and in how they are charged and displayed, making them hard for tenants to understand, find or compare across agents.

core_themes.name: Tenant powerlessness in agent selection
core_themes.claim: Because landlords, not tenants, appoint and pay the agent, tenants have little or no control or ability to negotiate or opt out of the fees charged to them.

core_themes.name: Weak competitive pressure on tenant fees
core_themes.claim: Landlords and agents have little incentive to keep tenant fees low (and may even keep landlord fees down by raising tenant fees), so competitive pressure on tenant-facing fees is very weak, explaining their rise and variation.

core_themes.name: Scale and growth of fees
core_themes.claim: Tenant fees are often substantial (commonly £200-£300 but sometimes far higher) and have risen significantly faster than general costs in recent years.

core_themes.name: Financial and behavioural harm to tenants
core_themes.claim: High, repeated and often hidden up-front fees create real financial hardship for tenants, deter house moves, encourage short-term lets, and make it harder to save for a home deposit.

core_themes.name: Failure of existing transparency regulation
core_themes.claim: Existing transparency requirements under the Consumer Rights Act 2015 have not succeeded in enabling tenants to shop around or driving up standards, demonstrating that lighter-touch regulation is insufficient to solve the problem.

core_themes.name: Redressing landlord market power
core_themes.claim: Because landlords choose and can negotiate with agents while tenants cannot, banning tenant fees shifts the cost to the party (landlords) who actually has market power to discipline agents' charges.

core_themes.name: Transparency through all-in pricing
core_themes.claim: The ban will let tenants see at a glance the true all-in cost of a property via the advertised rent, improving their ability to compare and choose properties.

core_themes.name: Insufficiency of transparency-only reform
core_themes.claim: Because transparency requirements alone have failed to improve the market, a full ban rather than further disclosure rules is the necessary and chosen remedy.

core_themes.name: Scottish precedent as supporting evidence
core_themes.claim: Experience from Scotland's long-standing ban shows that banning tenant fees has had minimal negative effects on the sector and some positive effects on competition, supporting the case for an English ban.

core_themes.name: Scope of the ban and treatment of deposits
core_themes.claim: The ban should cover all fees that effectively charge tenants for granting, renewing or continuing a tenancy, while allowing tenants to continue paying rent and a (possibly capped) refundable deposit.

core_themes.name: Acceptable trade-off of rent increases
core_themes.claim: Although landlords may pass some agent costs into higher rents, this is an acceptable and more transparent outcome compared to hidden tenant fees.

core_themes.name: Local authority/Trading Standards enforcement
core_themes.claim: The ban should be enforced primarily by local authorities' Trading Standards teams, building on their existing enforcement role for redress and transparency requirements.

core_themes.name: Tenant empowerment and education
core_themes.claim: Educating and empowering tenants to recognise and challenge unlawful fees is a necessary complement to formal enforcement, reducing the burden on local authorities.

core_themes.name: Possible lead enforcement authority
core_themes.claim: Drawing on the Estate Agent sector's model, a designated lead enforcement authority could provide consistent central oversight and support for local enforcement of the ban.

core_themes.name: Data sharing between bodies
core_themes.claim: Improved data and intelligence sharing between Trading Standards, redress schemes and professional bodies would strengthen enforcement against non-compliant agents.

core_themes.name: Penalties calibrated to deter non-compliance
core_themes.claim: Non-compliance should be met with a civil penalty (potentially higher than the current £5,000, up to £30,000) or criminal/banning-order route, to provide a credible deterrent.

core_themes.name: Defined exceptions to the ban
core_themes.claim: Certain charges—holding deposits and tenant-caused in-tenancy charges—should remain permissible, with safeguards such as refunds and possible caps, to keep the ban workable without harming legitimate practice.
